title: The war is pushing Iran closer to Russia
gist: Chatham House argues the US-Israeli war on Iran (begun 28 Feb 2026) is moving Tehran from scepticism to viewing Russia as a strategic necessity, evidenced by three October meetings and reported Russian intelligence and components. Benefits are real but not a game changer, with institutionalised military cooperation the most durable outcome.

insights.claim: In October 2026 Iranian and Russian senior officials held three high-level meetings: Pezeshkian-Putin on 8 October in Turkmenistan, Lavrov in Tehran on 19 October, and Pezeshkian in Moscow on 27 October.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Signals intensifying Iran-Russia alignment during the war.

insights.claim: Araghchi said never in Iran-Russia history have the two worked as closely as now, and Pezeshkian thanked Russia for wartime support.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Public tone from Iran's political and security leadership has turned markedly warmer.
insights.quote: never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now

insights.claim: Meeting substance was not much different from earlier exchanges apart from nuclear work; the notable change is the more positive public tone, which does not necessarily mean all Iranian decisionmakers have changed their views.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Tone shift is a signal, but do not overread it as unanimous consensus.

insights.claim: Putin said bilateral trade rose 10.4 per cent in the first eight months of 2026, and reaffirmed projects including Bushehr nuclear plant.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Trade is growing despite the war, though the base is not given.

insights.claim: Rosatom said it would raise construction workers at Bushehr to 200 after having evacuated staff when the war began.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Concrete sign Russian commercial presence in Iran is returning.

themes.theme: Why Tehran's scepticism of Moscow is fading

insights.claim: The US-Israeli war, which began 28 February 2026, is changing Tehran's view of Russia from an unreliable partner that benefited disproportionately to an important partner for military survival, reconstruction and long-term deterrence.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Core thesis: structural shift in Iranian strategic alignment.

insights.claim: Iranian scepticism of Russia grew from late 2022 as some questioned returns on supporting Russia's Ukraine war, including thousands of Shahed-131/136 drones supplied.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Explains the prior ceiling on the partnership.

insights.claim: Leaked contracts indicate Russia agreed to pay about $290,000 per drone for 2,000 Shahed-136s, though completion of payments is unclear; Iran reportedly helped set up production of the Geran-2 variant in Russia.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Russia's drone production is partly Iranian-derived; payments uncertain.

insights.claim: Critics in Tehran said Russia sought to drag Iran into the Ukraine war to increase sanctions pressure on Iran, and feared Moscow would use Iran as a bargaining chip with Washington.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Historic distrust remains a latent constraint.
insights.quote: There is a view that Russia sought to drag Iran into that [Ukraine] war

insights.claim: Tehran felt Russia gave little help in the June 2025 12-day war with Israel and did not deliver advanced systems such as SU-35 fighters that Iran said it had purchased.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Past non-delivery is the key credibility gap for Russia.

insights.claim: Reports say Russia gave Iran intelligence on US military positions, satellite imagery for targeting and weapons components, contradicting Trump's claim that Moscow and Beijing have not helped Tehran.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Direct Russian involvement raises US-Russia friction risk; real battlefield impact is hard to assess.

insights.claim: The wartime support vindicates the security-establishment faction, backed by the late president Raisi, that argued Russia ties help circumvent sanctions, end diplomatic isolation and counter Western pressure.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Hardliner faction strengthened in Iranian policymaking.

insights.claim: Closer cooperation with Russia will likely be seen as a strategic necessity rather than merely a means of sanctions circumvention, with support broadening across the Iranian political spectrum.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Alignment becomes less dependent on any single faction.

insights.claim: Short term, Russian technical help and components could sustain Iranian capabilities degraded by months of fighting, help rebuild air defences, missile infrastructure and defence industry, and aid tracking of US assets.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Raises Iran's resilience and costs to adversaries if escalation resumes.

insights.claim: Russian support is unlikely to fundamentally alter the balance of power in Iran's favour.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Caps the upside of the Iran-Russia axis for escalation scenarios.
insights.quote: unlikely to fundamentally alter the balance of power in Iran’s favour

insights.claim: Medium term, assuming the war ends, cooperation will likely focus on air defence, drones and missile technology, e.g. S-300 replacement components and electronic warfare tech, though Russia is constrained by Ukraine war demands on its defence industry.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch for S-300 and EW transfers as indicators.

insights.claim: Longest-term, the most consequential outcome could be institutionalised Iran-Russia military cooperation in planning, procurement and defence-industrial work, making the partnership harder to reverse regardless of who holds power, despite no binding security guarantee.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Durable axis reduces effectiveness of US military and economic pressure at the margin.
insights.quote: harder to reverse, no matter who is in power
